stem: In the admin portal, which job belongs to Entra ID and which to the Node API?
options: Entra ID proves who the user is and issues a token; the API decides what that user may do, using the roles in the token
Entra ID decides which API endpoints each user may call; the API only checks the password
The API proves who the user is by checking the password hash; Entra ID decides permissions
Entra ID does both, so the API needs no checks at all
explanation: Entra ID authenticates and issues a signed token that carries claims such as app roles. Authorisation - whether this user may refund an order - is the API's decision, made from the validated token. An API that skips its own checks trusts any caller who reaches it.

scenario: After adding Entra ID sign-in, the React portal sends the token it received at sign-in to the Node API, and every request fails with 401.
options: The API needs a client secret to read tokens
The portal is sending its ID token, whose audience is the portal; it must request an access token whose audience is the API
Entra ID tokens cannot be used with Node.js
The user has not completed MFA
explanation: An ID token tells the front end who signed in and is addressed to the front end. APIs accept access tokens issued for them, and a correct API rejects anything whose audience is not its own. MSAL requests the access token by naming the API's scope.

scenario: The nightly integration that posts orders to the warehouse system stopped at 03:00. The app registration's client secret, created two years ago, expired at midnight.
stem: What is the best long-term fix?
options: Create a new secret with the longest expiry allowed and set a calendar reminder
Store the secret in Key Vault so it cannot expire
Run the integration with a managed identity (or workload identity federation outside Azure) so there is no secret to expire
Share the admin portal's secret with the integration so there is only one to manage
explanation: Secrets expire by design and live in config somewhere. A managed identity has credentials Azure rotates for you, and workload identity federation lets GitHub Actions or another cloud get tokens without a stored secret. Key Vault stores secrets safely but does not stop them expiring, and sharing secrets widens the blast radius.

scenario: The shop has 40 staff and no Entra ID P1 licences. After the finance director's account was taken over, Priya wants MFA for everyone this week.
stem: What is the fastest sound step?
options: Buy P2 licences and design a full set of Conditional Access policies before enabling anything
Turn on security defaults, which require MFA for everyone and block legacy authentication at no cost
Ask staff to use longer passwords
Enable MFA only for the finance director
explanation: Security defaults give MFA for all users and block legacy protocols with one switch and no licence. Conditional Access with P1 adds finer rules later. Longer passwords do nothing against reuse, and protecting one user leaves the next phishing target open.

scenario: A new Conditional Access policy requiring a managed device was applied to all users on Friday evening. Nobody's laptop meets the rule yet, and now no administrator can sign in.
options: Two emergency access accounts excluded from all policies, and testing the policy in report-only mode first
Giving every administrator a second account in the same policy
Using security defaults instead of Conditional Access
Raising a Microsoft support ticket in advance
explanation: Report-only mode shows who a policy would block before it blocks anyone, and emergency access accounts - excluded from every policy, alerted on use - exist for exactly this lock-out. A second admin account under the same policy is locked out too, and support recovery takes days.

scenario: Ana proposes signing the React Native app's customers up as users in the staff tenant, so the shop only runs one directory.
options: Agree, and put customers in a separate group
Keep customers in the admin portal's own users table
Use a separate Microsoft Entra External ID tenant for customers, with its own sign-up, social logins and branding
Invite each customer as a guest user
explanation: Customers need self-service sign-up, social and one-time-code sign-in and a branded experience, and they must never sit alongside staff who have access to internal systems. External ID provides exactly that in its own tenant. A home-grown table means owning password storage and reset, and guest invitations are for business partners.

scenario: A contractor who left three months ago can still sign in to the Azure portal. He had been given an account in the shop's tenant, with a password, when he joined.
stem: How should contractors be handled from now on?
options: Continue creating accounts, but share one account between all contractors
Invite them as guest users who sign in with their own company's identity, with access that expires or is removed by access review
Give them the Owner role only on weekends
Keep their accounts but remove MFA so they are easier to disable
explanation: Guests authenticate with their own organisation, so you hold no password for them, and an expiry date or access review removes the access without relying on someone remembering. Shared accounts destroy accountability, and removing MFA makes the account easier to steal.

scenario: The API checks whether a user may refund orders by looking for a group ID in the token's groups claim. It works for most staff, but a senior manager in 230 groups is always refused.
options: Remove the manager from some groups
Hard-code the manager's user ID in the API
Define an app role such as Orders.Refund, assign a group to it, and check the roles claim
Switch the API to read the ID token instead
explanation: Beyond 200 groups, Entra ID replaces the groups claim with an overage pointer, so group checks silently fail. App roles are defined by the application, assigned to groups, and arrive as a short roles claim - and the API checks a meaningful name rather than an opaque group ID. The ID token is not meant for APIs at all.
